paragraphs: Before we go on to examine any other objections to an indefinite power of taxation in the Union, I shall make one general remark. If the jurisdiction of the national government in the matter of revenue were restricted to particular objects, it would naturally cause an undue proportion of the public burdens to fall on those objects. Two evils would spring from this source: the oppression of particular branches of industry, and an unequal distribution of the taxes, both among the individual States and among the citizens of the same State.

Suppose that the federal power of taxation were confined to duties on imports, as has been contended for. It is evident that the government, for want of other resources, would often be tempted to extend these duties to an injurious excess. There are persons who imagine that these duties can never be carried too far, since the higher they are, the more, it is alleged, they will tend to discourage extravagant consumption, to produce a favorable balance of trade and to promote domestic manufactures. But all extremes are harmful in various ways. Exorbitant duties on imported articles would breed a general spirit of smuggling, which is always prejudicial to the fair trader and eventually to the revenue itself. They tend to make other classes of the community tributary, to an improper degree, to the manufacturing classes, to whom they give a premature monopoly of the markets. They sometimes force industry out of its more natural channels into others in which it flows with less advantage. And in the last place, they oppress the merchant, who is often obliged to pay them himself without any repayment from the consumer. When demand equals the quantity of goods at market, the consumer generally pays the duty; but when the markets happen to be overstocked, a great proportion falls on the merchant, and sometimes not only exhausts his profits but breaks into his capital. I am inclined to think that a division of the duty between the seller and the buyer happens more often than is commonly imagined. It is not always possible to raise the price of a commodity in exact proportion to every additional imposition laid on it. The merchant, especially in a country of small commercial capital, is often under a necessity of keeping prices down in order to sell more quickly.

The maxim that the consumer is the payer is so much more often true than the reverse that it is far more equitable for the duties on imports to go into a common stock than to benefit the importing States exclusively. But it is not so generally true as to make it equitable for those duties to form the only national fund. When the merchant pays them, they operate as an additional tax on the importing State, whose citizens pay their share of them as consumers. In this view they produce inequality among the States, and that inequality would grow as the duties grew. Confining the national revenues to this kind of impost would also bring inequality, from a different cause, between the manufacturing and the non-manufacturing States. The States that can go farthest toward supplying their own wants by their own manufactures will not, in proportion to their numbers or wealth, consume so great a share of imported articles as the States that are not in the same favorable situation. They would not, therefore, by this means alone contribute to the public treasury in proportion to their abilities. To make them do so, it is necessary to have recourse to excises, whose proper objects are particular kinds of manufactures. New York is more deeply interested in these considerations than those of her citizens who contend for limiting the power of the Union to external taxation may be aware. New York is an importing State, and is not likely soon to be, to any great extent, a manufacturing State. She would, of course, suffer in a double way from restraining the jurisdiction of the Union to commercial imposts.

As far as these observations tend to show a danger of the import duties being extended to an injurious extreme, it may be observed, in line with a remark made in another part of these papers, that the interest of the revenue itself would be a sufficient guard against such an extreme. I readily admit that this would be the case as long as other resources were open. But if the avenues to them were closed, HOPE, stimulated by necessity, would produce experiments, fortified by rigorous precautions and additional penalties, which for a time would have the intended effect, until there had been leisure to devise expedients to elude these new precautions. The first success would be apt to inspire false opinions, which it might take a long course of later experience to correct. Necessity, especially in politics, often brings about false hopes, false reasonings, and a system of measures that is erroneous accordingly. But even if this supposed excess should not follow from limiting the federal power of taxation, the inequalities I have spoken of would still ensue, though not in the same degree, from the other causes I have noticed. Let us now return to the examination of objections.

One objection, which if we may judge by how often it is repeated seems to be the one most relied on, is that the House of Representatives is not numerous enough to admit all the different classes of citizens, so as to combine the interests and feelings of every part of the community and to produce a due sympathy between the representative body and its constituents. This argument presents itself in a very specious and seductive form, and is well calculated to take hold of the prejudices of those to whom it is addressed. But when we dissect it with attention, it will appear to be made up of nothing but fair-sounding words. The object it seems to aim at is, in the first place, impracticable, and in the sense in which it is contended for, unnecessary. I reserve for another place the discussion of the question whether the representative body is sufficient in numbers, and shall content myself here with examining the particular use that has been made of the contrary supposition in relation to the subject immediately under inquiry.

The idea of an actual representation of all classes of the people by persons of each class is altogether visionary. Unless the Constitution expressly provided that each different occupation should send one or more members, the thing would never take place in practice. Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to give their votes to merchants in preference to persons of their own professions or trades. These discerning citizens are well aware that the mechanic and manufacturing arts furnish the materials of mercantile enterprise and industry. Many of them, indeed, are directly connected with the operations of commerce. They know that the merchant is their natural patron and friend, and they are aware that, however great the confidence they may justly feel in their own good sense, the merchant can promote their interests more effectively than they can themselves. They are aware that their habits in life have not been such as to give them those acquired endowments without which, in a deliberative assembly, the greatest natural abilities are for the most part useless. They are aware too that the influence, weight and superior acquirements of the merchants make them better able to contend with any spirit that might happen to infuse itself into the public councils, unfriendly to the manufacturing and trading interests. These considerations, and many others that might be mentioned, prove, and experience confirms it, that artisans and manufacturers will commonly be disposed to give their votes to merchants and to those whom the merchants recommend. We must therefore consider merchants as the natural representatives of all these classes of the community.

With regard to the learned professions, little need be observed. They truly form no distinct interest in society, and according to their situation and talents will be indiscriminately the objects of the confidence and choice of each other and of other parts of the community.

Nothing remains but the landed interest. In a political view, and particularly in relation to taxes, I take this to be perfectly united, from the wealthiest landlord down to the poorest tenant. No tax can be laid on land that will not affect the owner of millions of acres as well as the owner of a single acre. Every landholder will therefore have a common interest in keeping the taxes on land as low as possible, and common interest may always be reckoned on as the surest bond of sympathy. But even if we could suppose a distinction of interest between the wealthy landholder and the middling farmer, what reason is there to conclude that the first would stand a better chance of being sent to the national legislature than the last? If we take fact as our guide and look into our own senate and assembly, we shall find that moderate owners of land prevail in both. This is no less the case in the senate, which consists of a smaller number, than in the assembly, which is composed of a greater number. Where the qualifications of the electors are the same, whether they have to choose a small or a large number, their votes will fall on those in whom they have most confidence, whether these happen to be men of large fortunes, or of moderate property, or of no property at all.

It is said to be necessary that all classes of citizens should have some of their own number in the representative body, so that their feelings and interests may be better understood and attended to. But we have seen that this will never happen under any arrangement that leaves the votes of the people free. Where the votes are free, the representative body, with too few exceptions to have any influence on the spirit of the government, will be composed of landholders, merchants and men of the learned professions. But where is the danger that the interests and feelings of the different classes of citizens will not be understood or attended to by these three kinds of men? Will not the landholder know and feel whatever will promote or secure the interest of landed property? And will he not, from his own interest in that kind of property, be sufficiently inclined to resist every attempt to harm or burden it? Will not the merchant understand, and be disposed to cultivate as far as may be proper, the interests of the mechanic and manufacturing arts, to which his commerce is so nearly allied? Will not the man of a learned profession, who will feel neutral toward the rivalries between the different branches of industry, be likely to prove an impartial arbiter between them, ready to promote either so far as it appears to him to serve the general interests of society?

Take into account the passing moods or dispositions that may happen to prevail in particular parts of society, to which a wise administration will never be inattentive. Is the man whose situation leads him to wide inquiry and information less likely to be a competent judge of their nature, extent and foundation than one whose observation does not travel beyond the circle of his neighbors and acquaintances? Is it not natural that a man who is a candidate for the favor of the people, and who depends on the votes of his fellow citizens to continue in public honors, should take care to inform himself of their dispositions and inclinations, and should be willing to allow them their proper degree of influence on his conduct? This dependence, and the necessity of being bound himself and his posterity by the laws to which he gives his assent, are the true and strong chords of sympathy between the representative and the constituent.

There is no part of the administration of government that requires so much extensive information and thorough knowledge of the principles of political economy as the business of taxation. The man who understands those principles best will be least likely to resort to oppressive expedients, or to sacrifice any particular class of citizens to the procurement of revenue. It might be demonstrated that the most productive system of finance will always be the least burdensome. There can be no doubt that, for a judicious exercise of the power of taxation, the person in whose hands it is placed must be acquainted with the general character, habits and modes of thinking of the people at large, and with the resources of the country. And this is all that can reasonably be meant by a knowledge of the interests and feelings of the people. In any other sense the proposition has either no meaning or an absurd one. And in that sense, let every considerate citizen judge for himself where the requisite qualification is most likely to be found.
